catalog_quote: In disyllabic words of the shape (C)VC(C)V(C) containing only short peripheral vowels, the basic stress pattern in Tape is for stress to be attached to the penultimate syllable. ... With words which contain a mix of schwas and peripheral vowels, the position of stress varies somewhat from the penultimate placement of stress described so far. With disyllables ... in which the vowel of the initial syllable is schwa and the vowel of the second syllable is not schwa, stress is generally attracted instead to the final syllable. ... When a vowel is available for deletion according to the generalisations presented in §5.1.1.3, it never receives stress, even if it is retained and it appears in the penultimate syllable. ... The schwa is simply ‘bypassed’ for stress assignment purposes, meaning that [*i'msit] is not a possible pronunciation. ... when the penultimate syllable contains a schwa and the remaining syllables contain other vowels, stress shifts one syllable to the left to the antepenultimate syllable if that syllable contains a peripheral vowel. ... Stress in Tape is not fixed to a particular syllable of a root in all morphological contexts. Given that the addition of prefixes and suffixes can affect the number of syllables in a word, stress can be shifted leftwards or rightwards from a particular syllable in the root in line with the general requirement that stress should ordinarily appear on the penultimate syllable of the phonological word.
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (217 PDF pp., text layer present, no scanned) and the ANU text bundle. Title page and CIP entry (PDF pp. 1-6) confirm it is Crowley, Terry, ed. John Lynch, 'Tape: a declining language of Malakula (Vanuatu)', Pacific Linguistics 575, ISBN 0 85883 567 3, 2006. Note: the PDF's embedded metadata title reads 'Naman: a vanishing' (a leftover from the sister volume PL 576, Crowley 2006c); the content is unmistakably the Tape grammar. Both quoted passages are present verbatim: p. 104 (PDF p. 122), first paragraph under the heading '5.2 Stress': 'In disyllabic words of the shape (C)VC(C)V(C) containing only short peripheral vowels, the basic stress pattern in Tape is for stress to be attached…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress falls on the penultimate syllable of the phonological word (root plus affixes), and moves with affixation to stay penultimate. Syllable counting is adjusted: a sequence of two adjacent vowels at the end of a word counts as one syllable (so stress lands on the syllable before it, e.g. ['niniu]), while a word-final syllabic /l/ or /n/ produced by schwa loss counts as a syllable. Schwa is skipped when it is deletable: in CəCV(C) disyllables stress goes to the final syllable ([nə'mi] 'dust', with weakly marked and sometimes variable stress), in longer words with a schwa penult it goes to the antepenult if that has a peripheral vowel ([po'tandəlin] 'his/her neck'), and a prefix takes the stress rather than a deletable root schwa (['imsit] 'he is sick'). Words containing only schwas, or schwa plus a medial cluster, take regular penultimate stress. Vowel length (phonemic status uncertain) does not affect placement.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned anywhere in §5.2 or elsewhere in the grammar.
new_statements.exceptions: (i) CəCV(C) disyllables: stress attracted to the final syllable, phonetically weak and with recorded variation between first and second syllable ([tsə'nin ~ 'tsənin] 'his/her intestines'). (ii) Words ending in VV or VVC with a preceding CV syllable: the VV counts as one syllable, stress on the preceding syllable; but if that preceding syllable has schwa, stress goes to the first of the two vowels ([m̃ə'liun] 'chief'). (iii) Longer words with a schwa penult: stress shifts to the antepenult. (iv) Deletable schwa never bears stress even if retained in the penult.
new_statements.domain_note: Phonological word (root plus prefixes and enclitic-like suffixes). Possessum + nominal possessor sequences are 'stressed as two separate phonological words' (p. 125-126). Data are elicited citation forms and texts from about 15 elderly rememberers of a moribund language (salvage description; Crowley died before completing it, Lynch edited).
new_statements.identity_note: Crowley's 'Tape' is the same language Glottolog lists as Maragus (mara1399, ISO mrs). Crowley 2006:3-4 states that Marakus/Maragus/Maragaus (Deacon 1934; Capell & Layard 1980; Tryon 1976) is the Naman-language exonym Maraakhus 'bush person', not a Tape word, and that today's speakers call the language Tape. Data are from the last ~15 elderly speakers resettled at Tautu village, northwestern-central Malakula; no dialect distinctions are described. Grambank codes mara1399 from the same grammar.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress falls on the penultimate syllable of the phonological word (root plus affixes), counted with these adjustments: (a) a word-final VV(C) sequence counts as one syllable when a CV syllable precedes it, so stress goes on the preceding syllable; in a bare CVV(C) disyllable the first vowel is stressed; (b) a word-final syllabic /l/ or /n/ from schwa loss counts as a syllable; (c) in CəCV(C) disyllables (schwa in the first syllable, peripheral vowel in the second, no medial cluster) stress is generally on the final syllable, with occasional variation; a deletable schwa is never stressed and is bypassed (/i-msit/ -> ['imsit]); (d) in trisyllables with schwa in the penult and peripheral vowels elsewhere, stress moves to the antepenult; (e) with a medial consonant cluster stress is invariably penultimate even on schwa. Vowel length does not affect placement.
new_statements.exceptions: Schwa-driven shifts (final in CəCV(C), antepenult when the penult is schwa), bypass of deletable schwa, VV sequences counted as one syllable; the phonetic stressed/unstressed difference in CəCV(C) words 'is, in fact, not particularly marked' with variation such as /cənin/ [tsə'nin ~ 'tsənin]. Stress is reassigned when affixes change the syllable count (root /lis/: ['lis], ['ilis], [i'lisər]).
new_statements.identity_note: Crowley 2006 (printed p. 1, PDF p. 19) states that Tape 'has been referred to elsewhere in print (Deacon 1934; Capell & Layard 1980:4; Tryon 1976) as Marakus, Maragus and Maragaus', and (printed p. 6, PDF p. 24) that Tryon 1976 contains 'a basic wordlist of about 200 items.. where the language was referred to as Maragus'. Tryon's Maragus (list 95/96, collector DT, Malekula) is therefore the same language as Tape/mara1399. Crowley's description is a salvage description of a moribund language from a handful of speakers; no dialect distinction is made.
